title: Dictionaries
description: Store pairs of keys and values so you can look a value up by name instead of by position.

content.value: In a list you find an item by its position. That works when order is what matters, but it is hopeless for a phone book: nobody remembers that their friend is number 14. A dictionary links a key, such as a name, to a value, such as a number, so you look things up by the key instead of by counting.
You write a dictionary with curly braces. Inside, each pair is a key, a colon, then its value, and the pairs are separated by commas.

Square brackets do all three jobs. With a key that already exists you read its value, or assign to replace it. With a key that does not exist yet, assigning creates the pair. Every key can only appear once, which is why assigning to an existing key overwrites instead of adding a second copy.

hero = {
    "name": "Peter Parker",
    "power": "Spider webs"
}

hero["power"] = "Shooting spider webs"   # key exists, so this replaces
hero["city"] = "New York"                # new key, so this adds a pair
print(hero)
When the Key Is Not There

Reading a key that does not exist does not give you a blank or a None. It stops the program with a `KeyError`. When you are not certain the key is there, `.get()` is the safe version: it hands back None instead of raising an error, and you can give it a fallback value to use instead.

hero = {"name": "Peter Parker"}

# print(hero["age"])            # KeyError, the program stops here
print(hero.get("age"))          # None, no crash
print(hero.get("age", "unknown"))   # unknown, your own fallback
You can also ask before you look: `if "age" in hero:` is True only when that key exists. For a dictionary, `in` checks the keys, never the values.
Looping straight over a dictionary gives you the keys, one at a time, and you can use each key to reach its value. When you want both at once, `.items()` hands you the pair together.
Both loops print the same two lines. Choose the second when you need the value as well, because it saves looking each one up again.

quiz.question: Which brackets make a dictionary?
quiz.explain: Dictionaries use curly brackets. Square brackets make lists, parentheses make tuples.

quiz.question: In the pair "name": "Batman", which part is the key?
quiz.explain: The part before the colon is the key you look things up with. "Batman" is the value it points to.

quiz.question: hero holds only "name". What does  print(hero["age"])  do?
options: Stops the program with a KeyError
quiz.explain: Reading a missing key is an error. hero.get("age") is the version that hands back None instead of stopping.
